title: Victoria Sponge
subtitle: The classic British sandwich cake with jam and cream
excerpt: Two light, golden sponge cakes sandwiched with raspberry jam and whipped cream. Simple and precise. Beloved across Britain since the Victorian era. The benchmark of home baking.

recipe.sourceNotes: Victoria sponge is named after Queen Victoria, who is said to have enjoyed a slice with her afternoon tea. The cake became popular in Britain after baking powder was commercialised in the 1840s, which made the light, airy texture possible without laborious hand-beating. The traditional Women's Institute recipe uses equal weights of butter, sugar, flour, and eggs. The all-in-one method, where everything is beaten together, became popular in the 1960s with the widespread adoption of electric mixers.

content.text: All ingredients should be at room temperature: cold butter and eggs will not cream properly. Divide the batter between the two tins by weight for the most even layers. The cakes are done when they are evenly risen, golden, and spring back when pressed lightly in the centre. Do not open the oven in the first 15 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180 C / fan 160 C / gas 4. Grease and line the bases of two 20 cm sandwich tins.

Beat the butter and caster sugar until very pale and fluffy, about 4 minutes. Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each. Add the vanilla. Fold in the flour and baking powder. Add the milk and mix until smooth.
Divide evenly between the two tins. Level the surfaces. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes until risen, golden, and a skewer comes out clean. Cool in the tins for 5 minutes, then turn out onto a rack.
Spread the jam over the flat side of one cooled sponge. Spread the whipped cream over the jam. Place the second sponge on top, flat-side down. Dust with icing sugar.
